topic.title: What is a cache and why does it make software faster?
topic.scope: Explain that a cache is a nearby temporary copy of data that was already fetched or computed, so software can reuse it instead of repeating slow work, and what trade-off comes from the copy going stale.

analogy.click: The first time you need something that lives far away, you pay the full slow trip. If you keep a copy close by, every later time is instant. But the copy never updates itself, so when the original changes, the copy quietly goes out of date.
brainstorm: Making a spare house key instead of borrowing the original from the landlord's office each time
Taking a photo of the fridge shelf before shopping so you needn't call home about eggs
Putting leftover soup in the fridge instead of cooking a new pot each night
Deli sandwiches pre-made in the display case instead of built to order
Photographing the meeting-room whiteboard instead of walking back to look at it
Keeping the water pitcher on the dinner table instead of walking to the tap each refill
Keeping a stash of snacks in your desk drawer instead of walking to the far pantry
Memorizing your shortcut to work after figuring it out once, until a road closes
Pre-chopping vegetables on Sunday for the whole week, until they wilt
Carrying a spare phone charger in your bag instead of going back home for it
Setting out a tray of pre-poured drinks before guests arrive instead of mixing each one
Screenshotting a boarding gate screen so you needn't walk back to the monitor, until the gate changes
Putting the TV remote's spare batteries in the nearby drawer instead of the garage shelf

topic.title: What happens when you call an API?
topic.scope: Explain that an API is a defined way for one piece of software to send a structured request to another and get a structured response back, so programs can use each other's features without knowing how they work inside.

analogy.click: You can't walk into someone else's software and do the work yourself. They give you a fixed set of things you may ask for, in a fixed shape, and a go-between carries your ask in and brings a predictable answer back. You get the result without knowing or touching how it was made.

topic.title: Why does RAG split documents into chunks before searching them?
topic.scope: Explain that documents are cut into small passages so search can return only the specific piece that answers a question, since whole documents are too large and too vague to fit into a model's prompt.

analogy.click: One big whole is too large to hand over and too mixed to match to one specific need, so you cut it into small pieces that each hold one clear thing. Then you can pick just the piece that answers the need and hand over only that, which fits the limited space.

topic.title: What is DNS and how does a website name find its server?
topic.scope: Explain that DNS is the internet's lookup system that translates a human-readable domain name into the numeric address of the server hosting the site, so browsers know where to send their request.

analogy.click: A name is what people remember, but it can't tell you where to go. Before the trip starts, something looks the name up and hands back the exact numeric address, and only then can the visit begin.

topic.title: What is model routing, and why not use one AI for everything?
topic.scope: Explain that model routing is a step that looks at each request and sends it to the smallest model able to handle it, so simple tasks stay cheap and fast while hard ones go to a more powerful model.

analogy.click: Before any job gets done, someone looks at it and hands it to the cheapest helper that can handle it. The big expensive helper is saved for jobs only it can do. If everything goes to the big one, you pay and wait for nothing. If everything goes to the small one, the hard jobs fail.

topic.title: What is prompt injection, and why can it trick an AI?
topic.scope: Explain that a language model reads instructions and untrusted content as the same stream of text, so hidden commands inside a document or web page can be mistaken for real instructions and hijack its behavior.

analogy.click: The model takes in its owner's instructions and the material it was asked to read through the same channel. It acts on anything that looks like an instruction, so a command hidden in the material gets obeyed as if the owner gave it.

topic.title: What is a context window?
topic.scope: Explain that a context window is the fixed amount of text a language model can read at once, so anything beyond it, like the start of a long chat, is no longer seen when the model writes its answer.

analogy.click: The model never sees the whole conversation. Each time it answers, it reads only a fixed-size window of the most recent text. The window slides forward as the chat grows. Anything that slid out the back is not blurry or half-remembered. It is simply not in front of the model.

candidates.line: Your app asks the payment service every minute if anyone paid, and the answer is mostly no. How can it just be told?
candidates.question: How can it just be told?
candidates.why_it_pulls: Anyone running a store or app has wasted effort asking over and over for news that rarely comes, and wants a way to just be told.

candidates.line: Your app keeps asking a calendar service whether anyone booked, and most replies say nothing changed. How could it hear about bookings instantly?

candidates.why_it_pulls: Builders see the pile of empty replies in their logs and bills, and want the news to arrive on its own.
